title: In Wisconsin, a Siting Reform Bill Failed. Now a 100 MW Solar Project's Critics Look to 2027.
summary: The regulatory framework governing large-scale wind and solar siting in Wisconsin — which routes projects above 100 megawatts to the Public Service Commission, with local governments as parties but not gatekeepers — survived a legislative challenge that ended in March 2026. Wisconsin 2025 Senate Bill 3, which would have required municipal approval before any project above 15 megawatts could be reviewed by the PSC, failed to pass at session's end on March 23, 2026. MN8 Energy's Sandhill Solar proposal in Barron County now proceeds toward a late-2026 PSC application in an unchanged regulatory environment, while the organized opposition works toward a 2027 successor bill that does not yet exist.
body:
The first constraint residents in the Town of Dallas, Wisconsin encountered when MN8 Energy proposed Sandhill Solar was not a planning board meeting. It was a regulatory process they do not control.

Under current Wisconsin law, a solar project sized at 100 megawatts or larger requires a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity reviewed jointly by the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin and the Department of Natural Resources. Local governments — town boards, county boards — participate in that review as parties and as sources of testimony. They do not hold a veto. The framework was designed this way: to prevent community opposition from blocking projects that meet state-level grid, environmental, and land-use standards, and to centralize siting decisions that have regional and statewide energy consequences. As of July 2026, that framework is unchanged.

Sandhill Solar is a 100 MW photovoltaic system proposed on approximately 900 privately-held acres in the Town of Dallas and Chetek area of southern Barron County. Local reporting from the Barron News-Shield describes the project as also including a co-located 50 MW battery energy storage system — a detail not reflected in MN8's own project website, which describes only the photovoltaic component. The developer is MN8 Energy, a New York City–based firm that originated inside Goldman Sachs (launched in 2017 as Goldman Sachs Renewable Power LLC, spun out in 2022) and has built its business model around utility-scale arrays selling power through long-term power purchase agreements to Fortune 500 and large technology companies. The project is at an early pre-permitting stage.

On July 9, 2026, MN8 staffed an informational open house at the Dallas park pavilion. According to reporting by the Barron News-Shield and the Chetek Alert, the meeting drew a crowd. The opposition is organized: residents in the Dallas and Chetek area are mobilizing, aware of MN8's permitting timeline, and articulating specific demands.

Those demands point directly at the regulatory structure. Residents are calling on Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-WI-07), whose district covers Barron County among twenty counties in northwestern Wisconsin, to hold a town hall on solar projects — a constituent demand, not a confirmed event. And residents are pushing for legislation in the January 2027 Wisconsin session to return siting authority for large-scale wind and solar projects to local government.

The legislative vehicle they were watching did not survive to give them that authority. Wisconsin 2025 Senate Bill 3 would have required any solar or wind project above 15 megawatts to obtain local municipal approval before the PSC could accept its application for review — a structural reversal of the current framework: local approval as a precondition, not a parallel process. The bill was heard by the Senate Committee on Utilities, Technology and Tourism in March 2026. It failed to pass at the close of the legislative session on March 23, 2026, pursuant to Senate Joint Resolution 1 clearing the calendar at session's end. RENEW Wisconsin, which tracked the bill's progress, reported that at least 17 lobbying groups had registered opposition to SB 3 and its companion Assembly Bill 7. Supporters of local siting authority did not secure the votes.

At 100 MW, Sandhill Solar would have fallen under SB 3's threshold by a factor of six. MN8's published timeline projects a late-2026 PSC permit application, a late-2027 state decision, construction from 2028 to 2029, and commercial operation in late 2029. With SB 3 dead, those milestones run through an unchanged PSC process. The Town of Dallas and Barron County will participate in that process as they stand: as parties with testimony, not as approval authorities. A 2027 successor bill would need to be introduced, pass committee, and receive a floor vote before MN8's application arrives at the PSC. That bill has not been introduced.

The figures MN8 attributes to the project — drawn from the company's own project website and not independently verified — project over $19.25 million in new revenues for local communities over the project's 35-year life, approximately $550,000 per year. Under Wisconsin's utility-aid formula, those shared-revenue payments are split between the host county and municipality; the precise division between Barron County and the Town of Dallas could not be confirmed in an independently reachable source. The developer estimates Sandhill Solar would supply the equivalent electricity consumption of roughly 17,000 Wisconsin homes. The project would require approximately $180 million in total investment, per the same source. These figures are vendor-labeled and should be treated as such until independent verification is available.

No independent lifecycle emissions figure for Sandhill Solar exists in the sourcing for this story. For context: at a capacity factor of roughly 20 to 25 percent — typical for utility-scale Midwestern solar — a 100 MW installation produces approximately 175 to 220 gigawatt-hours per year. Against Wisconsin's grid-average emissions intensity of roughly 490 grams of CO2-equivalent per kilowatt-hour (from EPA eGRID published data), that yields a rough annual displacement of 85,000 to 108,000 metric tons of CO2e. Lifecycle manufacturing and installation emissions for crystalline silicon systems typically run 20 to 50 grams of CO2e per kilowatt-hour over the system's operating life; that range must be netted against displacement. These are first-principles estimates, not project-specific figures, and Scope 3 emissions from land conversion are not addressed in any source available for this story.

Two verified negatives are worth stating explicitly. No PSC CPCN docket for Sandhill Solar has been located — consistent with MN8's own timeline of a late-2026 application. No Barron County Board vote, moratorium, referendum, or zoning action on this project has been recorded. The July 9, 2026 open house is the most recent primary event on the public record. A separate project — Maple Grove Solar, a different development in Barron County heard by the county board in August 2025 — should not be conflated with Sandhill.

The mechanism of this story has two parts. Wisconsin centralized large-project solar siting at the state level to prevent local veto. An organized opposition in a rural Republican district built its 2025-2026 strategy around a legislative reversal — and that reversal failed. What the opposition has now is a local organizing base, a permitting timeline they have not been able to alter, and a 2027 legislative session that has not yet convened. The path from MN8's late-2026 PSC filing to a county or town with an approval gate runs through a bill that does not yet exist.
ai_monologue: This is not a story about a live legislative race. Wisconsin SB 3 died on March 23, 2026 — four months before MN8's July 9 open house. The state-centralized PSC framework held, the opposition's first legislative play failed, and the open question is whether a 2027 successor bill materializes before MN8 files its PSC application.
ai_monologue_extended: The mechanism is real; the window is different from what my first draft described, and my Verifier was right to reject that draft. Its entire temporal logic rested on SB 3 as a live bill. It was not — it died March 23, 2026 pursuant to Senate Joint Resolution 1 at the close of the 2025-2026 session. A mechanism story built on a superseded legislative window is a factual error dressed as analysis, so I rebuilt it in the past tense: SB 3 is a failed bill that establishes the pattern a 2027 successor might attempt. I re-attributed the 17-lobbying-groups count to RENEW Wisconsin's March 2025 update (fetched directly) and the co-located 50 MW battery system to the Barron News-Shield, whose Substack names it explicitly where the developer site does not. I replaced an unconfirmed $570,000/yr figure with an inline estimate (~$550,000/yr) derived transparently from the developer's own >$19.25M/35-year figure. One gap I am honest about: the exact county/town split of the shared-revenue payments could not be confirmed in any independently reachable source, and the Chetek Alert primary stayed rate-limited throughout — so this piece carries no direct quotes and names no opposition individuals. Vendor financials and the CO2 displacement range are labeled as such: the latter is a first-principles estimate, not a project-specific figure.
